nota.t: Receptors detect stimuli; neurons carry impulses; effectors respond.

The nervous system has the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors, relay neurones process them and motor neurones carry them to effectors (muscles or glands).

v.c: The path of a nerve impulse

nota.t: Sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) detect stimuli. Responses are voluntary (controlled by the brain) or involuntary reflexes, such as pulling your hand from a hot object.

t: Sit with your leg hanging freely
Tap the tendon below the kneecap
The leg jerks forward by itself: a reflex

nota.t: Plants respond by tropisms: phototropism (shoots towards light), geotropism (roots downwards), hydrotropism (roots towards water) and thigmotropism (tendrils coil round supports). Nastic responses, such as the touch-me-not plant closing, do not depend on direction.
Breathing in: diaphragm contracts, chest volume increases.
The respiratory system: nasal cavity, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and lungs with alveoli. Alveoli have thin moist walls, a large surface area and many capillaries for efficient gas exchange.

Breathing in: intercostal muscles contract, ribs rise, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume increases and pressure falls, so air enters. Breathing out is the reverse. Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out.
Cigarette smoke (tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide), haze and dust damage the respiratory system, causing asthma, bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer.

Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels. By day photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so oxygen is released; at night only respiration happens and carbon dioxide is released. Other animals have adapted systems: gills in fish, tracheae in insects, moist skin in frogs.
Heart with 4 chambers; arteries, veins, capillaries.
Small organisms use diffusion; large multicellular organisms need transport systems because their surface area to volume ratio is small. Animals use blood circulation; plants use vascular tissue.

v.c: Surface area to volume ratio falls as size grows

nota.t: The circulatory system has the heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and blood. Humans have double circulation: pulmonary (heart → lungs → heart) and systemic (heart → body → heart). The heart has four chambers and valves.

t: Count your pulse for 1 minute at rest

r: thick wall, away from heart, high pressure
one cell thick, exchange of materials

nota.t: Blood is plasma (55%) and cells: red blood cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, white blood cells fight infection and platelets help clotting. ABO blood groups: A, B, AB and O; O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient.

Xylem carries water and mineral salts from roots to leaves; phloem carries the products of photosynthesis (translocation). Transpiration through stomata creates a transpirational pull and depends on light, temperature, wind and humidity.
K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > (C) > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au.
Metals below carbon are extracted with carbon; above it, by electrolysis.

Minerals are natural elements or compounds in the Earth's crust, such as bauxite, haematite, cassiterite and galena. The reactivity series orders metals by how readily they react with oxygen: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, Cu, Ag, Au.

v.c: Reactivity series (most reactive at the top)

nota.t: Metals less reactive than carbon (iron, tin) are extracted by heating the ore with carbon; more reactive metals (aluminium) are extracted by electrolysis.
Exothermic gives out heat; endothermic takes it in.

Exothermic reactions release heat (temperature rises): combustion, respiration, neutralisation. Endothermic reactions absorb heat (temperature falls): photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate, thermal decomposition.
Uses in daily life: hot packs (exothermic) and cold packs for sports injuries (endothermic), self-heating cans, and choosing fuels by their energy value.
Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Live brown, neutral blue, earth green-yellow.

Generators make electricity by turning a coil in a magnetic field (electromagnetic induction). Turbines are turned by steam (coal, gas, nuclear), water, wind or biomass. Renewable sources are kinder to the environment.
Transformers change a.c. voltage: step-up transformers have more secondary turns, step-down fewer. Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ.
Example: 240 V, Nₚ = 1 200, Nₛ = 60 → Vₛ = 12 V.
Electricity is sent through the National Grid at high voltage (275 kV or 500 kV) to cut energy loss, then stepped down at substations to 240 V for homes. Energy cost = power (kW) × time (h) × tariff.
Example: a 1 000 W iron for 30 min a day for 30 days = 15 kWh; at 21.8 sen = RM3.27.
W = Fd; P = W/t; Ep = mgh; Ek = ½mv².
Work = force × displacement (W = Fs), in joules. Power = work ÷ time (P = W/t), in watts.
Example: 50 N pushes a box 4 m in 8 s → work 200 J, power 25 W.

v.c: Work is done when a force moves an object

nota.t: Gravitational potential energy Eₚ = mgh; elastic potential energy is stored in stretched springs; kinetic energy Eₖ = ½mv².
Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m → Eₚ = 20 J. 2 kg at 3 m/s → Eₖ = 9 J.

v.c: Elastic potential energy in a spring

nota.t: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Examples: a pendulum (Eₚ ↔ Eₖ), a roller coaster and hydroelectric power.
Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay.

Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896; Marie and Pierre Curie found radium and polonium; Rutherford identified alpha and beta radiation. An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it; unstable isotopes are radioactive.

Ionising radiation (alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays) can ionise atoms and damage cells. Non-ionising radiation (radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light) is less harmful. Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by aluminium, gamma by thick lead.

Uses of radioactive radiation: medicine (radiotherapy, sterilising tools), agriculture (preserving food), industry (finding pipe leaks, measuring thickness), archaeology (carbon-14 dating) and nuclear power. Safety: film badges, protective clothing, warning signs.
Solar wind, sunspots and flares affect Earth; the magnetosphere protects us.
Sunspots, solar flares and coronal mass ejections release the solar wind. It causes auroras and can disturb radio, GPS, satellites and power grids. The Earth's magnetosphere protects us.

Space exploration grew from the geocentric model (Ptolemy) to the heliocentric model (Copernicus), telescopes (Galileo), Kepler's laws and Newton's gravity, with Muslim scholars contributing astrolabes and observatories. Today rockets, satellites, the ISS and space telescopes explore space; Malaysia sent its first astronaut in 2007.
